name: Overload past a safe limit
summary: A unit that takes over enemies has a safe number of captives but no hard cap, and it cannot stop itself from taking more. Past the safe number it overloads: it loses health at intervals, in steps that grow as its count passes a few set thresholds, until it is back at the limit because captives were spent in the fight, disposed of or lost. If the overload destroys it, every captive goes free. The rule turns its greatest strength into its counter: a swarm of cheap, expendable enemies makes it seize more than it can bear. A hard cap that simply stops new captures, or frees the oldest captive to make room, is a plain limit on mind control, not this pattern.
counterplay: Rush it with many cheap, expendable units so it takes more than it can hold and burns itself out.
While it is overloaded, leave its captives alive: every captive that dies brings it back toward its safe limit.
Hit it with units it can't take, such as crewless machines, aircraft, heroes or units another controller already holds, so the attack doesn't feed it.
Keep valuable units out of its reach until it is overloaded, then finish it.
Kill whatever keeps it alive: outside repair can out-heal the overload, so the repairers are the target.

other_examples.unit: Psychic Tower (Yuri), and the engine rule behind both
other_examples.note: For contrast, a hard cap from the same game: the tower holds up to three units and simply stops taking more, so the known answer is to fill its slots with cheap units and then destroy it with strong ones. By default the engine treats a controller's count as a hard limit, where it must free a captive to take a new one or takes none; a weapon flag replaces that with a list of thresholds that deal growing damage at set intervals, which is how the Mastermind overloads.

sources.title: Psychic tower, Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Its quote box copies the Yuri's Revenge manual entry for the structure.

other_examples.note: For contrast, no cap and no cost: each squad holds only one victim, but squads have no build limit, so in theory a player can hold any number of enemy units by building more squads.
For contrast, a hard cap that makes room: the number of persuaded creeps is capped by the ability's level, and persuading one more kills the oldest at once.

shooter_analogues.note: The same shape on heat instead of captives: a mech that reaches critical heat normally shuts down, but the pilot can override the shutdown for a few seconds and keep fighting while its internal structure slowly takes damage and stored ammunition may explode.

sources.title: Beginners Guide: Interface/Basics, MechWarrior Online Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: For contrast, a hard cap in a shooter: no more than seven thralls may exist at once, and each lasts only a set time.

player_translation.summary: A slow, heavily armoured T3 controller whose field takes the weapon of every enemy who walks into it, one after another, and can't be switched off. Three links are safe; each one past that drains your health faster, so you spend captives to cool down while the enemy team tries to feed you more than you can bear.
as_user: You buy a slow, tough T3 brain-tank with no gun. Every enemy who enters your field is linked on its own, and every linked weapon fires where you aim.
Up to three links are safe. A fourth starts the overload: your health drops in ticks that speed up with each extra link, and a big enough crowd finishes you in seconds.

You can't switch the field off or refuse a link. Your relief is to spend captives: press Q to make the nearest captive's weapon fire one last heavy burst and release it, or let your team kill captives.
Between fights you mend slowly; a repairer at your side lets you hold more for a while.
as_target: Walking into the field costs you your gun until you walk out of it or shake free (hold F); you keep moving.

The answer is a team plan: go in together with cheap units so it takes more than it can bear, and while it burns, keep linked teammates alive and inside, because every link it loses brings it closer to safety.
A counter over the controller shows its links against the safe limit; it turns red, sparks and rocks once it is overloaded.
teammates: The enemy team floods it with cheap units or several players at once, then finishes it with crewless machines or aircraft that it can't take.
The controller's team thins out swarms before they reach it, kills captives to bring it back under the limit and keeps a repairer on it.
controls: Move with WASD; the mouse aims every linked weapon at once and left mouse fires them.
The field is passive: links form on their own and there is no off switch.
Q: spend the captive nearest the cursor (one forced burst from its weapon, then it is released). One counted key and one passive, within the T3 budget.
Victims: hold F to break their own link; walking out of the field breaks it too.
feedback: A ring on the ground marks the field, with a link line to each captive.
A link counter above the controller, white up to the safe limit and red beyond it, with sparks, rocking and a voice line when the overload starts (as Red Alert 2 does).
A ticking sound that speeds up with each extra link, audible to both teams, so the swarm knows its plan is working.
changes_from_rts: Red Alert 2 gives no relief except captives dying or being recycled; a player needs a spend key, so the overload is a choice under pressure rather than only a death sentence.
Red Alert 2 captives stay until the controller dies; here a player who is linked keeps moving and can shake free or walk out, so the overload is a contest both teams play.
Show the safe limit and the current count on screen; the original hid the numbers, and sources still disagree on its safe limit (three in the game data, five in the launch profile).
Red Alert 2 raises the burn in a few steps, as the count passes set thresholds; here every extra link speeds it up, so each capture past the limit counts and both teams can hear it.
The top overload step in Red Alert 2 wrecks the tank almost at once; keep a last step that is fast but survivable for a moment, so the controller can react.
Linked weapons fire at the controller's cursor instead of giving full command of each captive.

team_play.notes: The enemy beats it with a plan (flood it with cheap units, then send immune ones), while its own team keeps swarms off it, culls captives and repairs it.

notes: A link counter and a table of damage steps are simple; the hard part is the many-link control it sits on (several hijacked weapons aimed by one player).
A spend key that picks the right captive under the cursor.
Edge cases: links lost while overloaded, overload under invulnerability (in Red Alert 2 the Iron Curtain paused it), healing received while overloaded.
UI on both sides: the counter, the safe limit and the overload state.
Too high a safe limit makes it an unbreakable wall; too low makes it useless.
A self-burn that the enemy can trigger can feel like a free kill; the spend key keeps the controller in charge of its fate.
Stacked outside repair can cancel the drawback (Red Alert 2 players kept an overloaded Mastermind alive by surrounding it with repair vehicles), so cap the healing it receives while overloaded.
Both teams need the link count and the safe limit at a glance.
It must be clear whether the controller is losing health to its own overload or to enemy fire.

variants.name: Escalating burn
variants.summary: Past the safe number, health drops in ticks that grow with each extra captive; back at the limit, the burn stops. Q spends a captive to cool down.

variants.name: Burnout release
variants.summary: When the overload destroys it, every captive is freed at once, so the enemy team gets all its units back in one moment.

variants.name: Repair-sustained
variants.summary: Outside repair can out-heal the burn, so a support teammate can keep an over-limit controller alive; the healing it receives while overloaded is capped, so the drawback never vanishes.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2 Mastermind kept alive by repair vehicles and an armour bonus

variants.name: No release
variants.summary: The pure original: no spend key, and relief comes only from captives dying or being disposed of, so the controller must lead its captives into the fight. Being passive, it can't share a card with the passive auto-capture field (a card has room for one passive), so it pairs only with a capture that uses a key and can pass the limit, such as spreading thralls or area seizure.

variants.name: Tipping point
variants.summary: A last threshold past which the burn is almost instant, so a big enough crowd destroys it outright.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2 Mastermind's top overload step

adds_strengths.why: No hard cap: it keeps taking enemies for as long as it can stand the overload.

adds_weaknesses.why: Past its safe number each extra captive burns its health faster, and it can't stop itself from taking more.

counters.why: A few valuable vehicles are the ideal haul: under the safe limit they cost it nothing.

countered_by.why: A rush of cheap, expendable units makes it take more than it can hold, so it burns itself out.
Crewless machines can't be taken, so they hit it without feeding it.
Fliers stay out of its field and attack it freely.

open_questions: Is this a pattern of its own or a variant of mind control? Among the pages read, only the Mastermind uses it; every other capped controller has a hard cap.
What should the safe limit be for a player unit, and should the enemy team see it?
Should the controller get a spend key (as proposed here), or is the no-relief original the point?

The generator's requires can name only mind-control, not one of its variants, yet the overload works only beside a variant that can hold more than the safe number at once (auto-capture-field, spreading-thralls or area-seize; weapon-puppet, lasting-link and leashed-parasite hold one victim, so it would never trigger). How should the generator pair them? Beside the passive auto-capture field it must also take the active kind (the Q spend key), since a card has room for one passive.

shooter_fit.reason: A built-in counter that the enemy team can plan around (flood it, then finish it with immune units), readable to both sides; it needs a spend key and a visible counter so the controller isn't simply executed.

review.notes: Re-checked field by field against its sources by the batch r1 checker, which covered all 33 batch patterns; research/r1/checker/checks.json lists every field and verdict. The wrong paths were fixed as the skeptic confirmed (cbe6de8).
